docs.title: Oncorix Field Reference Guide
docs.subtitle: For Pharmaceutical Sales Representatives — Internal Use Only

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
Oncorix is an oncology therapy approved for adult patients with advanced solid tumors. This reference guide consolidates the materials field representatives need most frequently: prior authorization process, dosing administration, the adverse event profile, patient assistance pathways, and approved responses to common field objections.

Reps should never offer medical advice or submit access paperwork on behalf of an office. Always refer clinical questions to medical affairs and direct office staff to the appropriate support program.

sections.heading: Prior Authorization Process
sections.body:
Prior authorization (PA) for Oncorix is required by most commercial and Medicare Part B plans for advanced solid tumor indications. The prescriber must supply: confirmed diagnosis with ICD-10 code and stage, biomarker testing results where indicated (HER2 status, MSI status), prior therapy history including progression on any first-line regimen, and the requested dosing schedule of 50 mg/m squared IV every 3 weeks.

Most payers respond within 5 to 7 business days. If denied, the appeal must include peer-reviewed literature supporting the use; the manufacturer's medical affairs team can supply a letter of medical necessity within 48 hours on request.

sections.heading: Dosing and Administration
sections.body:
Oncorix is administered as an IV infusion at 50 mg/m squared every 3 weeks for adult patients with advanced solid tumors. Premedication with a corticosteroid and antihistamine is required to reduce infusion-related reactions. Infusion duration is 60 minutes for the first cycle, 30 minutes thereafter if no reactions occurred.

Dose reductions for toxicity: first reduction to 40 mg/m squared, second to 30 mg/m squared; further reductions require discontinuation. Treatment continues until disease progression or unacceptable toxicity. No dose adjustment is required for mild renal or hepatic impairment; severe hepatic impairment is a contraindication.

sections.heading: Adverse Event Profile
sections.body:
The most frequently reported Oncorix adverse events from pivotal trial data: peripheral neuropathy (approximately 30% any grade, 8% grade 3 or higher), neutropenia (25% / 12% grade 3 or higher), fatigue (40%), nausea (35%), and infusion-related reactions in the first cycle (15%).

Grade 3 or higher peripheral neuropathy requires dose reduction per the dose-reduction algorithm in the prescribing information; persistent grade 3 neuropathy after dose reduction is a discontinuation criterion. Febrile neutropenia is a medical emergency and must be reported as a serious adverse event.

sections.heading: Patient Assistance Program
sections.body:
The manufacturer offers a patient assistance program for eligible Oncorix patients without insurance coverage or with high out-of-pocket costs. Eligibility: US residents, household income at or below 500% of the federal poverty level, and documented insurance denial or lack of coverage. Approved patients receive Oncorix at no cost, shipped directly to the treating institution.

The co-pay assistance program for commercially insured patients caps out-of-pocket cost at $25 per infusion, with an annual maximum of $25,000. Reps may direct offices to the access support hotline; reps must not enroll patients themselves or handle patient PHI.

sections.heading: Common Objections and Approved Responses
sections.body:
PA is too painful — direct the office to the manufacturer's PA support program, which provides electronic submission and PA specialists who follow up directly with payers; average approval time has dropped to 4 days.

My patients can't afford it — review the co-pay assistance program ($25 per infusion cap) and the PAP for uninsured patients.

I'm worried about peripheral neuropathy — reference the grade 3 management guide on the rep portal and offer to set up a peer-to-peer call with a medical science liaison.

I prefer once-weekly cisplatin — acknowledge clinician preference; the every-3-week Oncorix schedule reduces patient infusion-day visits by roughly two-thirds, a meaningful patient-experience differentiator for adherence and quality of life. Never disparage a competitor or make claims outside the FDA-approved label.

docs.title: ImmunoShield Access Guide
docs.subtitle: Prior Authorization and Patient Assistance — Internal Use Only

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body:
ImmunoShield is an immunology therapy indicated for rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and ulcerative colitis. Given the $4,500 per-unit acquisition cost, virtually every payer requires prior authorization and most patients benefit from one of the access programs described in this guide.

Reps should educate office staff on documentation requirements and direct patients to the access support team; reps must not submit PA paperwork or handle PHI.

sections.heading: Prior Authorization Process
sections.body:
ImmunoShield prior authorization is required by virtually every payer. Required documentation: confirmed autoimmune diagnosis with disease activity score, documented failure or intolerance of at least one TNF-inhibitor (mandatory step therapy in 90% of plans), hepatitis B and TB screening results within the past 6 months, and treatment goals.

Decisions typically take 7 to 14 business days. The manufacturer's PA support program provides electronic submission and dedicated PA specialists who follow up with payers; using this program has cut average approval time to 9 days.

sections.heading: Patient Assistance Programs
sections.body:
The ImmunoShield Patient Assistance Program (IPAP) provides ImmunoShield at no cost to uninsured or underinsured patients meeting eligibility criteria: US residents, household income at or below 400% of the federal poverty level, and no other coverage (private or public).

For commercially insured patients, the co-pay support card caps patient cost at $5 per infusion with an annual savings cap of $20,000. Government-insured patients (Medicare, Medicaid, TRICARE) are not eligible for the co-pay card. A foundation grant pathway exists for Medicare patients facing high coinsurance — refer the office to the access support team.

docs.title: Cardiozen Cardiology Field Brief
docs.subtitle: Dosing and Competitive Differentiation — Internal Use Only

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: Cardiozen is an oral cholesterol-lowering therapy with once-daily dosing, indicated as adjunct to diet for primary hypercholesterolemia. This brief covers the dosing protocol the field is asked about most often and the approved differentiation messaging against the leading external competitor.

sections.heading: Dosing and Titration
sections.body:
Cardiozen is dosed orally once daily. Starting dose is 10 mg for most patients. Titration to 20 mg may be considered after 4 weeks if LDL-C reduction targets are not met. Maximum dose is 40 mg daily.

No dose adjustment is required for mild to moderate renal impairment. In severe hepatic impairment, the drug is contraindicated. Cardiozen may be taken with or without food, but consistency improves adherence. Co-administration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors requires dose reduction to 5 mg daily.

sections.heading: Differentiation vs. External Competitor
sections.body:
Cardiozen differentiation versus the leading external competitor (referred to here as Product X): once-daily oral dosing versus Product X's twice-daily regimen; demonstrated 52% mean LDL-C reduction at 20 mg in the pivotal trial versus Product X's 41% at the equivalent dose; no required lipid panel monitoring after week 12 per the label, versus Product X's quarterly monitoring requirement; co-pay card with $0 minimum versus Product X's $25 minimum.

Reps must only compare on the approved messaging; off-label or unsupported comparisons are not permitted. The competitive grid on the rep portal is updated quarterly by medical affairs.

docs.title: Adverse Event Reporting Policy
docs.subtitle: Reporting Obligations for All Company Products

sections.heading: Reporting Requirements
sections.body:
Federal regulations and company policy require all employees, including sales representatives, to report any adverse event they become aware of, for any company product, within 24 hours.

This includes events reported informally during a sales call, mentioned by office staff, or seen in public posts on social media. Failure to report can result in regulatory action against the company and disciplinary action against the rep.

sections.heading: What to Capture
sections.body:
When reporting an adverse event, include: patient initials (if known), age range, the product involved, the event itself, and any outcome. Do not request additional clinical details from the source; medical affairs will follow up directly.

Reports may be submitted via the AE reporting form on the rep portal or by calling the medical information line. Both routes are equally valid; use whichever is faster from the field.

sections.heading: Common Questions
sections.body:
Do I report secondhand reports? Yes — if you become aware of an event from any source, including office staff or social media, you must report it within 24 hours.

Do I follow up with the patient or HCP? No. Medical affairs handles all follow-up. Your obligation ends at submission.

What if I'm not sure it qualifies as an AE? Err on the side of reporting. The triage team will determine whether the case meets the regulatory definition of an adverse event.

sections.heading: Commercial Payer Status
sections.body:
As of the most recent quarterly update, Cardiozen is on the preferred tier (Tier 2) for the three largest commercial payers in the Northeast region.

UnitedHealthcare requires step therapy through atorvastatin. Aetna requires step therapy through any high-intensity statin. Blue Cross Blue Shield of Massachusetts has no step therapy requirement and accepts Cardiozen as a first-line option for hyperlipidemia patients.

sections.heading: Medicare Part D Status
sections.body: Medicare Part D plans in the region place Cardiozen on Tier 3 with prior authorization. The PA criteria are aligned with the commercial payer criteria but typically require explicit documentation of statin intolerance or inadequate response to maximally tolerated statin therapy.

sections.heading: Field Implications
sections.body:
Reps in the Northeast should lead with the BCBS-MA story when calling on accounts with high BCBS-MA mix — the absence of step therapy is a significant differentiator versus the rest of the regional payer mix.

For accounts with primarily UnitedHealthcare or Aetna patients, the conversation should pivot to the manufacturer's PA support program, which has cut the average approval turnaround for these payers to under 5 business days.
